sections.heading: What is Big-O?
sections.content: Big-O notation describes how the time or memory used by an algorithm grows as the input size n grows. It ignores constants and small terms, so 3n + 10 is simply O(n). In interviews, Big-O usually means the worst case unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: Rules for Calculating Time Complexity
items: Drop constants – O(2n) becomes O(n)
Drop lower-order terms – O(n² + n) becomes O(n²)
Sequential steps add – O(a + b)
Nested steps multiply – O(a * b)
Halving the problem each step gives O(log n)
Use different variables for different inputs (n and m)

sections.heading: Example: Add vs Multiply

rows.situation: New array, list or map of size n

sections.heading: Remember the Call Stack
sections.content: Recursion always uses stack space. A recursive DFS on a skewed tree uses O(n) space, not O(1). Always count the stack when you state space complexity.

sections.heading: Amortized Complexity
items: Some operations are occasionally expensive but cheap on average
ArrayList.add() is O(1) amortized – resizing is rare
StringBuilder.append() is O(1) amortized
Building a heap from n items is O(n), even though each push is O(log n)

Other Common Pitfalls
items: Sorting inside a loop turns O(n log n) into O(n² log n)
Chained map / filter / sorted calls each create a new list
Use asSequence() for long chains on large data
Comparing two strings with == costs O(length)

sections.heading: Memoization Shortcut
sections.content: With memoization, each unique state is computed only once. So time complexity = (number of states) × (work per state).

sections.heading: Worked Example: Two Sum
Trade-off Explained
sections.content: Brute force Two Sum uses two nested loops: O(n²) time and O(1) space. The HashMap version is O(n) time and O(n) space. You trade memory for speed, and you should say this out loud in interviews.

sections.heading: Interview Checklist
items: State both time and space complexity every time
Name your variables clearly (n = length, m = columns)
Mention the time vs space trade-off when you optimize
Include recursion stack in space complexity
Watch for hidden costs: contains, substring, += on strings, removeAt(0)
Match the constraints to the target complexity table before coding

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Big-O describes growth rate, not exact speed
Drop constants and lower-order terms
Sequential adds, nested multiplies, halving gives log n
Know the cost of the Kotlin collection operations you use
Use input constraints to pick the approach: n ≤ 10⁵ means aim for O(n log n) or better
